title: Understanding the menstrual cycle
body:
Your menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. The average cycle lasts around 28 days, but anything from 21 to 35 days is common and healthy.

The cycle is often described in two halves. The first half (the follicular phase) runs from day one until ovulation, when an egg is released from the ovary. The second half (the luteal phase) runs from ovulation until your next period and is usually fairly stable at 12 to 14 days.

Tracking your cycle over several months helps you spot your own rhythm. Because cycles vary from person to person and month to month, patterns only emerge with consistent logging.

This article is for general education only and is not a medical diagnosis. If your cycles are very irregular, extremely painful, or suddenly change, talk to a healthcare professional.

title: The four phases of your cycle
body:
The menstrual cycle is traditionally divided into four phases.

Menstruation (days 1 to 5 on average) begins when the lining of the uterus sheds. Many people feel cramping and fatigue during this time.

The follicular phase follows, overlapping with menstruation and continuing until ovulation. Rising estrogen helps rebuild the uterine lining and often brings a welcome boost in energy and mood.

Ovulation usually happens around day 14 in a 28-day cycle. The mature egg is released, and some people notice a brief twinge, lighter discharge, or a slight temperature rise.

The luteal phase runs from ovulation to the next period. Progesterone peaks, which can lead to PMS-like symptoms such as bloating, breast tenderness, and mood changes.

Learning which phase you are in can help you understand your energy, appetite, and mood patterns throughout the month.

title: What is the fertile window?
body:
The fertile window is the span of days when pregnancy is possible. Sperm can survive inside the body for up to five days, and the egg lives for roughly 12 to 24 hours after release.

That means the fertile window extends about five days before ovulation plus the day of ovulation itself. For most people this is roughly days 9 to 14 of a typical 28-day cycle, but the exact timing depends on your personal cycle.

Apps like Witchy estimate the window from your logged cycle lengths. These estimates are most reliable for people with regular cycles and become less certain when cycles are irregular.

Predictions are educational estimates, not medical advice, and are not a reliable method of contraception. If you want to use fertility awareness for birth control, work with a clinician who can teach you the full symptothermal method.

title: Signs that ovulation is approaching
body:
Several physical changes can hint that ovulation is near.

Cervical mucus often becomes clear, stretchy, and slippery, like raw egg white, in the days before ovulation. This fertile mucus helps sperm travel and is one of the easiest signs to observe.

Basal body temperature dips slightly just before ovulation and then rises about 0.3 to 0.5 degrees and stays elevated until the next period. Taking your temperature at the same time each morning makes this pattern visible.

Other possible signs include mild pain on one side of the lower belly, a heightened sense of smell, and increased libido.

No single sign is foolproof. Combining calendar estimates with mucus and temperature observations gives a far clearer picture, which is the basis of the symptothermal method.

title: Early signs of pregnancy
body:
The most reliable early signal is a missed period, but many people notice symptoms before that point.

Breast changes, such as tenderness, heaviness, or darkening of the areola, can begin within one to two weeks of conception. Fatigue is another very common early complaint, driven by rising progesterone.

Nausea, sometimes called morning sickness, usually begins around week six, though it can appear earlier and at any time of day. Frequent urination, mild cramping, and light spotting known as implantation bleeding can also occur.

Many of these symptoms overlap with PMS, so on their own they are not proof of pregnancy. A home pregnancy test taken from the first day of a missed period is the practical next step, and a positive result should be confirmed by a healthcare provider.

title: How your cycle affects your sleep
body:
Hormonal changes across the cycle can subtly shift your sleep.

During the follicular phase, rising estrogen supports lighter, more refreshing sleep and higher daytime energy. Around ovulation, sleep is often at its best.

In the luteal phase, higher progesterone can make you feel drowsy, but the accompanying rise in body temperature may make sleep less deep and more broken. Some people report more vivid dreams or a feeling of waking unrefreshed in the days before their period.

Practical help includes keeping a consistent sleep schedule, limiting caffeine in the afternoon, and keeping your bedroom cool, especially in the premenstrual week. If sleep problems are severe or persistent, discuss them with a doctor, as sleep disorders can affect anyone regardless of cycle phase.

title: Coping with period cramps
body:
Menstrual cramps are caused by prostaglandins, chemicals that make the uterus contract to shed its lining. They are one of the most common period symptoms.

Simple measures can help. Applying a heating pad or hot-water bottle to the lower belly relaxes the muscles and often brings quick relief. Gentle exercise such as walking, stretching, or yoga improves blood flow and can reduce discomfort.

Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen work best when taken at the first sign of pain, because they block the prostaglandins that drive cramping. Staying hydrated and cutting back on salt and caffeine may also soften symptoms.

Cramps that are severe, get worse over time, or interfere with school or work deserve medical attention. Conditions such as endometriosis can cause intense pain and benefit from early diagnosis.

title: PMS vs. PMDD: knowing the difference
body:
Many people feel physical and emotional changes in the week before their period. This is premenstrual syndrome, or PMS, and it is very common.

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder, or PMDD, is a much more severe form. PMDD involves intense mood symptoms, such as irritability, anxiety, and depression, that disrupt daily life and relationships, and they typically improve soon after the period starts.

Tracking symptoms alongside your cycle is one of the best tools for spotting the pattern. Note when symptoms start, how intense they are, and when they ease. A consistent luteal-phase pattern over several months is a strong clue.

If your premenstrual symptoms feel overwhelming, you are not alone and help is available. A doctor or mental health professional can discuss treatment options, including lifestyle changes, therapy, and medication.
